title: Subha and the stranger
hookLine: a man blocks Subha's path in a mango grove, praising her eyes; she shows him what an eye is (Therigatha, Subha)
last: SO IT WAS, SO IT IS.

lines: WHAT WRONG HAVE I DONE YOU?
cards: A path through a mango grove, the one known as Jivaka's. A nun named Subha is walking it. A man steps into her way and stays there.
What wrong have I done you, she asks, that you stand in my path? It isn't fitting for a man to touch a woman who has gone forth. He doesn't step aside.
He starts talking instead: about her youth, about the forest in flower, and more than anything, about her eyes.

teach.h: A HOUSE, CLOTH, AND HER EYES.
teach.b: First, his pitch. He offers her a life of comfort: fine cloth, ornaments, a house, the grove in bloom and full of birdsong. Give up the robe, he says.
And he keeps returning to her eyes, like a doe's, he says; nothing is dearer to him. Second, her answer. Subha takes his praise apart.
What is this body you're so taken with? What is an eye?

teach.h: A BALL IN A HOLLOW, WITH TEARS.
teach.b: A little ball set in a hollow, she says, with a bubble in the middle and tears around it. She compares a body to a painted puppet. She has seen through what he's selling.
Third, the act. Then the poem does something startling.
She plucks out her eye and holds it out to him: here, take it. His desire vanishes on the spot. He asks her forgiveness, wishes her well, and lets her go.
Subha goes on to the Buddha, and the poem says that when she saw him, her eye was restored as it had been.

What to make of a story like this? Some readers hear renunciation pushed to its limit. Others hear a woman refusing to be reduced to a part of her body: he wanted the eye, so she showed him what an eye is.
The poem tells it once, as her answer, not as a thing anyone is asked to repeat. And its first line still stands on its own: she names the wrong plainly, before anything else happens.

how: Contemplating the parts of the body is a traditional Buddhist practice for loosening desire, and teachers sometimes tell Subha's story to show that practice used as a clear refusal.

o: the eye, and the seeing it does

games.q: Subha in the grove: tap the pairs.
p: praises her eyes, like a doe's

s: Subha flatters the man so he'll let her go
she names the wrong plainly, then shows him what an eye is.
in the poem, her eye is restored when she sees the Buddha
the poem ends with her eye made whole as it had been.
the man keeps pursuing her afterward
his desire vanishes; he asks her forgiveness and wishes her well.

games.q: you're Subha, walking alone in a mango grove. a man blocks your path and praises your eyes. what do you do?
o: step around him and take another path.
ask what wrong you've done, and show him what an eye is.
agree to hear him out later.
games.why: she names the wrong, takes his praise apart, and in the poem holds out her own eye. his desire is gone, and he asks forgiveness.

practice: Bring to mind one unwanted pull, a sales pitch, a tug from your phone, a habit of saying yes, and hear Subha's first question: what wrong have I done, that you stand in my path? Let a no form, plain and unhurried.
If someone is truly blocking your path the way the man in the grove did, that calls for more than a breath: tell someone you trust.

wordCard.voice: Cakkhu. The eye: the word behind Subha's question to a stranger who praised her eyes on a forest path, what is an eye? Today's word.

orig.note: Pali cakkhu: the eye. The stranger praises Subha's eyes; she shows him what an eye is.

carryVoice: Your line: what is an eye. Her first words named the wrong, plainly. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 2 (Samannaphala Sutta, set in Jivaka's mango grove at Rajagaha)
